The S&P 500 index is down 6% from its October high while AI stocks are down 30%+ from their highs. The equal-weighted S&P 500 index is down only 1.3% from its August high, and the S&P 500 ex-AI index is up 0.5%. There has been fierce rotation for months now, masking what might have seemed like a quiet trading range. History is full of episodes like this, where growing earnings take a backseat to tightening financial conditions. 

I suspect we will be in this mode for a while longer, not unlike 2018 or 2015. Friday’s modest recovery from Thursday’s 4% decline gave off a bit of a dead-cat vibe, which suggests to me that this rotation may not be over, even as many stocks remain in up-trends.  Last week’s purge felt a bit like the tariff tantrum growth scare of 2025, but that one was easily reversed by a policy pivot. I’m not sure that there’s a quick pivot to the current correction, other than a successful ANT IPO and the potential for a re-rating in the Mag 7 if investors decide that the incumbents will win in a scaled-back capex cycle. They have been significantly derated since their cash flows started going to capex instead of shareholders.

BREAKING: Total US consumer credit surged +$29 billion in September, to a record $5.19 trillion.

This marks the largest monthly increase since December 2025 and the 3rd-largest monthly increase since November 2023.

US consumer credit has now risen for 7 consecutive months by a total of +$125 billion.

Meanwhile, revolving credit, which includes credit cards, jumped +$16 billion, to a record $1.37 trillion, marking its largest monthly increase since November 2023.

Non-revolving credit, covering auto and student loans, rose +$12 billion, to $3.86 trillion, an all-time high.

US consumers are piling on debt to "fight" inflation.

US semiconductor stocks went from overbought to oversold in weeks:

The Semiconductor Index, SOX, fell -17% below its 200-day moving average on Thursday, its largest negative divergence since April 2025.

This is also the 2nd-largest such deviation since the 2022 bear market.

By comparison, during the 2008 Financial Crisis and following the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble burst, this metric dropped to -49% and -52%, respectively.

This marks a sharp reversal from June, when SOX traded +75% above its 200-day moving average, its largest positive deviation since 2000.

In other words, semiconductor stocks have shifted from extremely overbought to oversold territory in just 5 months.

Semiconductor stocks just saw one of their most violent swings in decades.

The scale of Big Tech's AI future financial obligations is extraordinary:

Alphabet, $GOOGL, Meta, $META, Anthropic, Microsoft, $MSFT, Amazon, $AMZN, Oracle, $ORCL, and Nvidia, $NVDA, have disclosed a combined $4.49 trillion in off-balance-sheet obligations.

These include future lease payments that have not yet commenced, data-center commitments, equipment purchases, and other contractual obligations.

Alphabet accounts for the largest amount, at $1.08 trillion, followed by Anthropic, at $865 billion, and Meta, at $810 billion.

By comparison, their combined on-balance-sheet obligations total just $758 billion, consisting of long-term debt and existing lease liabilities.

This means off-balance-sheet commitments are nearly 6 times larger than their on-balance-sheet obligations.

In total, these 7 tech companies face ~$5.25 trillion in combined financial obligations.

The AI infrastructure race is facing enormous future financial commitments.
